newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: MAN TAKES SLEDGEHAMMER TO AMERICA'S CUP IN NZ.
newsitem.headline: MAN TAKES SLEDGEHAMMER TO AMERICA'S CUP IN NZ.

text.p: A man wielding a sledgehammer on Friday badly damaged the Auld Mug, the America's Cup yachting trophy that Team New Zealand won in 1995, police said.
They said a man dressed in a suit walked into the Royal New Zealand Yacht Squadron in Auckland where the cup is housed, and went unchallenged to the room where the cup is displayed in a glass case.
The man pulled out the sledgehammer and began striking the glass case in a frenzied attack, police spokeswoman Joanne Gibbs said.
Gibbs said the man arrived at the squadron rooms at the Westhaven marina about noon, possibly with the sledgehammer hidden in his suit.
"The next thing they know he is smashing at the cabinet the cup is in. He has been arrested and is helping us down at central (station) with our inquiries," Gibbs said.
The man was slightly injured by broken glass from the cup cabinet.
Police did not identify the man but described him as a Maori whom they believed to be some sort of activist. They did not say if any charges had been filed against him.
A spokesman for the Royal New Zealand Yacht Squadron said the cup was badly damaged around the mid section.
"It is quite extensively damaged to the main centre piece."
No estimate of the damage was immediately available, but the cup was insured for US$2 million when it was held by the San Diego Yacht Club.
Sir Peter Blake, who masterminded the Team New Zealand challenge to wrest the cup from the San Diego Yacht Club in May, 1995, was reported to be devastated by the attack.

Club commodore John Heise said Sir Peter was "understandably shocked and dismayed, particularly that we have gone out of our way to make the cup available to New Zealanders who want to look at the cup". Other trustees had been inclined to lock it away.
"We have taken the attitude that it is New Zealand's cup and New Zealanders can look at it. It is very disappointing that something like this can happen to it."
Heise said it was sickening to see the badly damaged cup lying half in and half out of the case.
The cup was likely to be sent back to the manufacturers, Garrards, in England, for repairs. He said the company apparently still had the original drawings of the trophy, which was made about 1850.
Heise said until it was sent back to Garrards, it was impossible to say if the cup could be successfully restored.
The Auld Mug is up for grabs again in the year 2000.
